builder_plan.scenario: A support or data assistant repeats work across related customer requests.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's memory change in a replay of past tasks, with separate memory per customer.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current memory pipeline plus a no-memory control using the same agent.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Task success, stale memories, retrieval misses, response latency, and all memory maintenance costs.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Route to Remember: Adaptive Memory Selection for LLM Agents
summary: The method replaces per-query retrieval of accumulated textual memory with knowledge internalized into model weights via on-policy self-distillation, plus a verify-then-regenerate router that falls back to text memory when weight memory is uncertain. It costs a per-user or per-domain fine-tuning pipeline (teacher-student training of the same model), ongoing retraining as facts accumulate, and added routing complexity, though it reduces tokens read per query at inference. It can fail on episodic facts not yet distilled into weights, on stale knowledge after user data changes, and on router misjudgments that answer from weights when retrieval was needed.
rationale: The approach is plausible on constrained infrastructure since it trains a context-free student from the same model rather than a foundation model, but its per-user fine-tuning cost and the single-benchmark evidence require workload-specific validation before production adoption.
technique: Weight memory via on-policy self-distillation with router

claims.statement: The method replaces per-query retrieval of accumulated textual memory with knowledge internalized into model weights via on-policy self-distillation, plus a verify-then-regenerate router that falls back to text memory when weight memory is uncertain. It costs a per-user or per-domain fine-tuning pipeline (teacher-student training of the same model), ongoing retraining as facts accumulate, and added routing complexity, though it reduces tokens read per query at inference. It can fail on episodic facts not yet distilled into weights, on stale knowledge after user data changes, and on router misjudgments that answer from weights when retrieval was needed.

On the HaluMem benchmark, OPSD matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines, including full-context prompting and retrieval systems, while reading fewer tokens per query; no numeric improvement factor is reported in the abstract.
